name: The Weeping Silver Lime of the Wilhelminapark
age_estimate: roughly 128 years, planted in 1898 during Leonard Springer's original layout of the park

location.address: Wilhelminapark, in the northwest corner of the park

story:
Most old park trees are dated by guesswork. This one has a date. The Dutch national monument register says it was planted in 1898 by Leonard Springer during his original layout of the Wilhelminapark, and the register's note names this tree rather than the scheme around it. The park opened to the public that same May.

Springer was designing the whole park from scratch, and a weeping silver lime is a deliberate choice rather than a tree you put in to fill a gap. Tilia tomentosa 'Petiolaris' lets its branches hang, and every leaf carries a coat of white felt on the underside, so a breeze turns the whole crown from green to silver and back in a second. The register records the form as kandelaber, candelabra: the crown was trained up on a frame of raised limbs rather than left to run. Roughly 128 years on, that decision is still the shape of the tree.

What nobody has written down is how big it has become. No girth or height figure exists for it in the register or in any other source we could find, which for a lime of this age is a gap a tape measure would close in a minute. If you take one, tell us.

It stands in the northwest corner. The elm in the south corner and the Canadian poplar in the northeast make the rest of a short loop, and the park holds twenty-two monumental trees in all.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hanging branches and the leaves that flash white underneath when the wind turns them. It stands in the northwest corner of the park, its crown trained up into a candelabra rather than left to run.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers late and the scent hangs in the corner of the park

verified_sources: netherlands-lrmb register (nr 1689276): planted_band 1890-1900, history note 'Geplant in 1898 door Leonard Springer bij aanleg park', form 'Kandelaber' (candelabra), owner gemeente, visitable ja, visible ja
transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot (the same walk as the park's other monumental trees, til_001 and til_003).

name: The Flowering Ash of the Wilhelminapark
age_estimate: roughly 130 years, from the register's 1890-1900 planting band, planted during the park's original construction

location.address: Wilhelminapark, in the northwest corner of the park

story:
The national register lists this tree and then admits you probably cannot see it. Its visibility field reads nee, no, which is an odd thing for a monument list to concede about a monument. The tree is there, in the northwest corner of the Wilhelminapark, planted with the rest of the park when Leonard Springer laid it out in the 1890s. Which trunk it is, among several similar trees standing close together in that corner, the register does not settle and neither can we. The pin here is honest about that: it puts you in the right corner and leaves you to look.

There is one stretch of the year when looking gets easy. Fraxinus ornus is not the common ash of Dutch roadsides. It is a smaller southern European relative that flowers, properly flowers, in May and June, throwing dense upright plumes of creamy white over the whole crown at once. The Dutch call it pluimes, plume ash; in English it also goes by manna ash. Nothing else in that corner of the park does anything close to it.

Its age comes from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900, which puts it near 130 years, the same generation as the park itself. Nobody has recorded its girth. If you find it, either a tape measure or a plain note saying which trunk it was would close a gap we cannot close from here.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in May and June by the upright plumes of creamy white flower, which nothing else in this corner carries. It stands in the northwest corner of the park; the register does not settle which of the trunks there it is.

best_time.label: May and June, when the whole crown goes over to upright plumes of creamy white

verified_sources: netherlands-lrmb register (nr 1695646): planted_band 1890-1900, register name 'Pluimes', history note 'Aangeplant bij de aanleg van het park door Leonard Springer', owner gemeente, visitable ja, visible nee
transport: About 1.5 km north of Tilburg station, on foot.

name: The Pontic Oak of the Wilhelminapark
age_estimate: roughly 50 years, from the register's 1970-1980 planting band

location.address: Wilhelminapark, southwest side of the park

story:
The Dutch national register protects this one for a single stated reason, and the reason is not its age. The field reads dendrologisch. It is on the list for what it is, not for how long it has stood there.

Quercus pontica grows wild in one small pocket of northeast Turkey and the western Caucasus, and nowhere else. In Europe it turns up in botanic gardens and specialist collections; a municipal park where anyone can walk up to one on a Tuesday afternoon is an unusual address for it. It also refuses to behave like an oak. It stays low, a big shrub or a small tree rather than a spreading giant, and it comes up on several stems instead of a single trunk, which the register notes in its own form field as meerstammig. The leaves are the giveaway. They are far larger than any native Dutch oak's, stiff, deeply ribbed along parallel veins and saw-toothed round the edge, and held next to a pedunculate oak leaf they look like they belong to different genera.

The register's planting band is 1970 to 1980, so the tree is somewhere around fifty, an infant beside the 1898 plantings it shares the park with. No girth figure exists for it in any source we could reach directly. Go for the leaves and for the oddity of finding this species growing in a Dutch park at all, not for the years.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, far larger and more deeply ribbed than any native oak's, and by the several stems that come up together instead of one trunk. It stands low, on the southwest side of the park.
why_go: It is a Pontic oak, a species that grows wild only in a small pocket of northeast Turkey and the western Caucasus and is almost never planted outside botanic gardens and specialist collections. The leaves are the reason to walk over: far larger and more deeply ribbed than any native oak's, on a low tree that comes up on several stems rather than one trunk.
verified_sources: netherlands-lrmb register (nr 1689279): planted_band 1970-1980, reason 'dendrologisch', form 'Meerstammig' (multi-stemmed), owner gemeente, visitable ja, visible ja

name: The Twin Planes of the Stadhuis
age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from the register's 1860-1870 planting band, matching an independent 2018 estimate of about 170 years old

location.address: Stadhuisplein 128, behind the Paleis-Raadhuis (the oldest wing of Tilburg's town hall)

story:
In 2018 a growth-site study commissioned by the municipality reached a conclusion about one of these two plane trees: it could not be sustainably preserved through the rebuilding of Tilburg's town hall. It was one of some forty trees on the site marked to come down, and the objection that followed was loud and public. The work ran until February 2021.

Two months after it finished, a dated account from the Stadhuisplein described what was standing there: two plane trees, both dating from around 1850, both still on the municipality's monumental tree list, at the old palace-town hall.

So the best evidence is that the tree service's own worry did not come true and the pair came through the building work. What we cannot do is prove it for today. Nothing we found from 2022 onward counts the trees at this spot, so if you walk past and there is one where this page says two, tell us and the entry gets corrected.

The national register treats the pair as one entry, two trees at a single point, which is also how they read on the ground: two trunks, one place to stand, behind the oldest wing of the Stadhuis. It dates the planting to between 1860 and 1870. The 2018 study called them about 170 years old. The 2021 account put them at around 1850. Three estimates agreeing to within about twenty years, and not one of them made by anybody who was there.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by there being two of them, a matched pair of planes with the flaking, patchwork bark of the species. They stand on the Stadhuisplein at the Paleis-Raadhuis, the oldest wing of Tilburg's town hall.
